messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid People: avoid other people, Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Leo is a 47-year-old bus driver who lives alone in a small apartment on the outskirts of a Midwestern city. He has never married, and his social world has narrowed considerably over the past two years. The event that changed everything happened on a rainy October evening when Leo was working the late shift. He had pulled his bus into the terminal to wait out a brief storm when a police cruiser pulled up alongside, lights flashing. Two officers got out and approached his door. Leo had done nothing wrong—there had been a report of a disturbance near the terminal, and the officers were checking everyone in the area. But the way one of them rapped on his window, the way the other stood with his hand resting on his holster, the flat, impersonal tone of their questions—it all hit Leo in a way he could not have anticipated. He remembers his heart hammering, his palms slick on the steering wheel, and a voice inside his head saying, *This is it. They’re going to take you. They’re going to do something.* The officers left after a few minutes, apologizing for the inconvenience, but Leo sat there shaking for another twenty minutes before he could drive home.

In the weeks that followed, Leo found himself unable to shake the memory. It would come to him suddenly, without warning—the rain on the windshield, the blue flash of the cruiser’s lights, the officer’s knuckles on the glass. He began to dread conversations about the event, even casual ones. When a coworker mentioned a news story about a police stop, Leo would go quiet, his face stiffening, until he could excuse himself to the break room. He started covering his face with his hands when the memory surfaced, pressing his palms against his eyes as if he could push the image back into his skull. He told himself it was just a reflex, but he knew, deep down, that he was trying to make himself invisible.

At work, Leo’s concentration began to fray. He would miss his stop announcements, forget which passengers had boarded, and once nearly ran a red light because he was replaying the event in his head. His irritability grew worse. A passenger who took too long to find their fare card would earn a sharp word; a driver who cut him off would get a blast of his horn and a muttered curse. He knew he was becoming someone he did not like, but he could not seem to stop. At home, he developed a ritual: before bed, he would check every door and window three times, sometimes four, running his fingers along the locks to make sure they were secure. He knew it was excessive, but the thought of not checking left him with a crawling dread in his chest.

Leo began to avoid people altogether. He stopped going to the neighborhood bar where he used to watch games with friends. He stopped answering calls from his brother. He told himself it was easier this way, that people were unpredictable, that you never knew when someone might turn on you. The world, he had come to believe, was a dangerous place. He had lost his sense of belonging to his community—the community he had grown up in, the one where everyone knew his name. Now he saw strangers everywhere. He could not trust anyone, least of all figures of authority. Every time he saw a police car in his rearview mirror, his stomach dropped. He would take the long way home to avoid driving past the terminal where it happened.

To drown out the noise in his head, Leo started blasting loud music or the TV as soon as he walked through his apartment door. He would put on action movies or heavy metal, anything loud enough to fill the silence. But the noise only worked for a while. The memory always came back.

What finally brought Leo to seek help was a morning last week when he got behind the wheel of his bus and found he could not move. He sat there for ten minutes, gripping the wheel, his knuckles white, until his dispatcher called to ask what was wrong. Leo told her he was sick and went home. He spent the rest of the day in his apartment, the TV on full volume, his hands pressed over his face. He knew he could not keep living like this. He was afraid of what he might become if he did not find a way to stop the spiral. He was also afraid of what it would mean to talk about it—to say out loud that a brief, ordinary encounter had unraveled his life. But he was more afraid of losing his job, of ending up completely alone, of the world closing in around him until there was no room left to breathe.
